We discuss principles for design and evaluation of verifiers, and introduce SGV, a method that improves verification by harnessing MLLMs' own capabilities via modulation of (un)conditional generation. First, an MLLM generates broad priors about desired behavior, independent of the data under evaluation. Then, conditioned on generated priors, it reasons over and judges a candidate trajectory. Our methods yield more human-aligned verifiers, with gains of up to 25pp in failure detection, 14pp in accuracy, and benefits extending to downstream applications. In self-improvement and online supervision, our verifiers boost task completion of a GUI specialist in OSWorld, a diffusion policy in robomimic, and a ReAct agent in VisualWebArena--surpassing the previous SOTA by 20pp. Finally, we release an updated version of Vis

signals.title: PAC Reasoning: Controlling the Performance Loss for Efficient Reasoning
signals.summary: arXiv:2510.09133v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress in complex problem-solving tasks. Despite this success, LRMs typically suffer from high computational costs during deployment, highlighting a need for efficient inference. A practical direction is to switch the LRM between thinking and non-thinking modes dynamically. However, such approaches often introduce additional reasoning errors and lack statistical guarantees for the performance loss, which are critical for high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Reasoning that controls the performance loss under the user-specified tolerance. Specifically, we construct an upper confidence bound on the performance loss and determine a threshold for switching to the non-thinking model. Theoretically, using the threshold to switch between the thinking and non-thinking modes ensures bounded performance loss in a distribution-free manner. Our experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method can save computational budgets and control the user-specified performance loss.

signals.title: Flow Reconstruction from Sparse Measurements in Urban Drainage Networks: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of Data-Driven Sparse Sensing
signals.summary: arXiv:2511.04556v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Urbanization and increasingly frequent intense storms are placing stress on urban drainage networks. While dense monitoring is desirable, practical constraints in time, budget, and technology hinder its full implementation. How to monitor and predict flow conditions across the entire network under constrained resources is a major challenge. To address this, we evaluated data-driven sparse sensing (DSS), which selects sensor locations and reconstructs network-wide flow from the same reduced basis, in a 76-conduit urban drainage network. Simulations of a calibrated SWMM model were used to construct an event-weighted spatial basis using singular value decomposition (SVD), select rank-specific layouts using pivoted QR, and define the reconstruction decoder. Applied to 225 held-out simulations combining 25 plausible calibrated parameter sets with nine rainfall events, monitoring 5 of the 76 conduits (6.6%) achieved a median system-level Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.992 (10th percentile 0.973) for observed storms, and a median NSE of 0.967 at the active unmonitored conduits. Pivoted QR performed comparably to genetic-algorithm layouts without requiring iterative layout searches, whereas largest-upstream-area placement failed with the DSS decoder and trailed QR even with a weighted regression decoder. The DSS flow reconstruction performance was insensitive to prescribed multiplicative Gaussian measurement noise, additive noise up to about 2 L/s and a 10 L/s detection floor, but showed location-dependent responses to loss of a monitored conduit, which a refitted regression decoder largely removed. This study supports the use of DSS, driven by physics-based simulations, for deciding how many flow sensors to install and

signals.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Geometric Stability Analysis of Large Language Models in Chess Evaluation
signals.summary: arXiv:2512.15033v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated in chess by how closely their position evaluations agree with a strong engine, but such agreement does not show that a model evaluates equivalent positions consistently. We apply metamorphic relations to chess evaluation: a 180-degree rotation of pawnless positions, left-right mirroring, color swapping, position pairs one move apart, conversion between Forsyth-Edwards Notation and a natural-language description, and illegal positions. Six LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Chat, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5.1, Grok 4.1 Fast and Kimi K2 Turbo) evaluated seven test sets of 500 items each, with Stockfish 16.1 as the reference. All six models failed on rotation: at most 10.6% of the 500 rotated pairs received evaluations within 300 centipawns (cp) of each other, and the models often declared the legal rotated positions illegal. On the other four transformations, stability ranked the models as accuracy did except for the first two places: GPT-5.1 had the lowest mean stability error (186.17 cp) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 the lowest accuracy error (330.41 cp). Rejection rates for illegal positions ranged from 44.2% to 96.0%. Stability should be reported with the share of consistent pairs, because means over answered pairs concealed most rotation failures.

signals.title: Effect-Level Validation for Causal Discovery in Interactive Telemetry
signals.summary: arXiv:2602.08340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal discovery is increasingly used to analyze telemetry from interactive systems, but a plausible graph does not guarantee an identifiable or reliable product decision. We study this problem for one query: whether early competitive gameplay increases Day-1 retention in a deployed Role-playing game (RPG). We propose an admissibility-first framework that treats discovered graphs as structural hypotheses, keeps only graphs that identify the target effect and have adequate treatment-control overlap, and validates admissible effects through cross-algorithm stability, placebo, subsampling, and E-value diagnostics. On real telemetry, under minimal constraints the admissible runs that return Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) are those whose graphs leave player-versus-player (PvP) with no parents, so they estimate the confounded raw difference; under the full constraint set all are admissible. Runs returning Partial Ancestral Graphs (PAGs) are not evaluated by the DAG gate and are reported separately. The admissible DAGs agree on one adjustment set and return a positive, cohort-conditional risk-difference average treatment effect (ATE), down from a raw retention gap; the estimate keeps its sign under placebo and subsampling checks, but its magnitude changes with the adjustment set and the constraint specification. A known-truth simulation shows that the checks screen identification and stability given the measured variables and cannot certify the absence of unmeasured confounding, and a second game-telemetry dataset shows that identifiability rates do not transfer. Graph-level recovery is therefore a weak proxy for causal reliability; discovery pipelines for decision support should be evaluated at the query and effect level.

signals.title: GT-HarmBench: Benchmarking AI Safety Risks Through the Lens of Game Theory
signals.summary: arXiv:2602.12316v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly capable and deployed in high-stakes multi-agent environments. However, existing AI safety benchmarks largely evaluate single agents, leaving multi-agent risks such as coordination failure and conflict poorly understood. We introduce GT-HarmBench, a benchmark of 1,535 high-stakes scenarios spanning game-theoretic structures such as the Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt and Chicken. Scenarios are drawn from realistic AI risk contexts in the MIT AI Risk Repository. Across 15 frontier models, agents fail to choose socially beneficial actions in 39% of high-stakes cases, such as military escalation, election manipulation, and medical malpractice. We measure sensitivity to game-theoretic prompt framing and ordering, and analyze reasoning patterns driving failures. We further show that game-theoretic interventions improve socially beneficial outcomes by up to 31%. Our results highlight substantial reliability gaps and provide a broad standardized testbed for studying alignment in multi-agent environments. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/Flecart/gt-harmbench.

signals.title: Legal interpretation and AI: from expert systems to argumentation and LLMs
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.05392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI and Law research has encountered legal interpretation in different ways, in the context of its evolving approaches and methodologies. Research on expert system has focused on legal knowledge engineering, with the goal of ensuring that human-generated interpretations can be precisely transferred into knowledge-bases, to be consistently applied. Research on argumentation has aimed at representing the structure of interpretive arguments, as well as their dialectical interactions, to assess of the acceptability of interpretive claims within argumentation frameworks. Research on machine learning has focused on the automated generation of interpretive suggestions and arguments, through general and specialised language models, now being increasingly deployed in legal practice.

signals.title: RewardFlow: Can Action-Level Reward Be Estimated from State-Graph Topology in Agentic RL?
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.18859v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In agentic tasks such as household assistance and web shopping, large language model (LLM) agents take multiple actions before receiving a final outcome indicating success or failure. For reinforcement learning (RL), this outcome obscures individual actions' contributions: a shopping trajectory may find the right product but fail to complete the purchase. To address this credit-assignment problem, we introduce RewardFlow, which connects multiple trajectories for the same task through shared states (states grouped by task-relevant equivalence or semantic similarity). The resulting directed state graph links observed trajectory segments. Therefore, an action in a failed trajectory may reach a state from which another trajectory succeeds. It propagates reward signals backward from states where the task succeeds, assigning state potentials that decrease with shortest-path distance to success in the graph. Potential differences then reward actions that reduce this distance, bringing the agent closer to success in the graph. These estimated rewards yield action-level advantages that complement trajectory-level advantages from outcome rewards during policy optimization, without a learned process reward model or manual action-level annotations. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban, and search tasks show gains over RL baselines across model scales. With 3B policies, graph construction and reward estimation take $1.47$-$2.39$ seconds per training step on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban (Fig. 1). Code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/RewardFlow.

signals.title: Understanding LLM Performance Degradation in Multi-Instance Processing: The Roles of Instance Count and Context Length
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.22608v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Users often rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) for processing multiple documents or performing analysis over a number of instances. For example, analysing the overall sentiment of a number of movie reviews requires an LLM to process the sentiment of each review individually in order to provide a final aggregated answer. While LLM performance on such individual tasks is generally high, there has been little research on how LLMs perform when dealing with multi-instance inputs. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive evaluation of the multi-instance processing (MIP) ability of LLMs for tasks in which they excel individually. The results show that all LLMs follow a pattern of slight performance degradation for small numbers of instances (approximately 20-100), followed by a performance collapse on larger instance counts. Crucially, our analysis shows that while context length is associated with this degradation, the number of instances has a stronger effect on the final results. This finding suggests that when optimising LLM performance for MIP, attention should be paid to both context length and, in particular, instance count.

signals.title: MonitorBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in Large Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2603.28590v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate chains of thought (CoTs) that are not always causally responsible for their final outputs. When such a mismatch occurs, the CoT no longer faithfully reflects the actual reasons (i.e., decision-critical factors) driving the model's behavior, leading to the reduced CoT monitorability problem. This limits the use of CoTs for reliable oversight. However, a comprehensive and fully open-source benchmark for thoroughly evaluating CoT monitorability remains lacking. To address this gap, we propose MonitorBench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating CoT monitorability in LLMs. MonitorBench provides: (1) a diverse set of 1,540 test instances with carefully designed decision-critical factors across 19 tasks spanning 7 categories to characterize when CoTs can be used to monitor the factors driving LLM behavior; and (2) two prompting stress-test settings to quantify the extent to which CoT monitorability can be degraded. Extensive experiments show that CoT monitorability is a conditional property affected by the evaluated LLM, monitor LLM, and task characteristics. Across these factors, monitorability is higher when decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning process, rather than merely influencing the final answer. Under stress-test prompting, most evaluated LLMs can intentionally reduce monitorability, mainly on tasks where decision-critical factors are not structurally required by the reasoning process. Overall, MonitorBench provides a basis for further research on AI control, reasoning faithfulness, stress-test monitorability, and monitoring scaffords. The code is available at https://github.com/ASTRAL-Group/MonitorBench.

signals.title: GrandCode: Achieving Grandmaster Level in Competitive Programming via Agentic Reinforcement Learning
signals.summary: arXiv:2604.02721v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Competitive programming remains one of the last few human strongholds in coding against AI. The best AI system to date still underperforms the best humans competitive programming: the most recent best result, Google's Gemini~3 Deep Think, attained 8th place even not being evaluated under live competition conditions. In this work, we introduce GrandCode, a multi-agent RL system designed for competitive programming. The capability of GrandCode is attributed to two key factors: (1) It orchestrates a variety of agentic modules (hypothesis proposal, solver, test generator, summarization, etc) and jointly improves them through post-training and online test-time RL; (2) We introduce Agentic GRPO specifically designed for multi-stage agent rollouts with delayed rewards and the severe off-policy drift that is prevalent in agentic RL. GrandCode is the first AI system that consistently beats all human participants in live contests of competitive programming: in the most recent three Codeforces live competitions, i.e., Round~1087 (Mar 21, 2026), Round~1088 (Mar 28, 2026), and Round~1089 (Mar 29, 2026), GrandCode placed first in all of them, beating all human participants, including legendary grandmasters. GrandCode shows that AI systems have reached a point where they surpass the strongest human programmers on the most competitive coding tasks.

signals.title: Submodular Benchmark Selection
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.02209v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating a new language model means running it on a large, growing collection of benchmarks, at considerable cost. Much of this cost is redundant: arranged as a matrix of models by benchmarks, scores are strongly correlated and concentrate in a few dimensions, so a few well-chosen benchmarks largely determine the rest. This allows us to run a new model on a few benchmarks and predict the rest with a simple Gaussian model that copes with missing scores. The key question is \emph{which few to run}. An answer comes from sensor placement, which chooses the observations that carry the most information, measured by entropy or mutual information. We argue that the objective should instead reward a selection for how well it predicts every benchmark. This leads to two coverage objectives: explained variance, the predictions' accuracy if the estimated correlations were exact, and facility location, which credits each benchmark with its best proxy among the selected ones. On eleven score matrices built from public evaluation results, the coverage objectives predict the scores of held-out models best wherever the correlations can be estimated. The information objectives fall behind because they favor benchmarks that the selection predicts poorly (entropy) or that the others predict well (mutual information), not benchmarks that predict the others. By contrast, facility location predicts practically as well as explained variance, holds up on the addition of newer models and under real costs, has classical guarantees (even under a budget), and gives readable selections.

signals.title: The Limits of AI-Driven Allocation: Optimal Screening under Aleatoric Uncertainty
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.07979v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rise of machine learning has shifted targeted resource allocation in policy and humanitarian settings toward algorithmic targeting based on predicted risk scores. This approach is typically cheaper and faster than traditional screening procedures that directly observe the latent vulnerability status through physical verification. Yet, even access to the true conditional vulnerability probability cannot eliminate misallocation: aleatoric uncertainty over individual vulnerability status is irreducible, and probabilistic targeting inevitably misallocates some resources. In this work, we study how screening and algorithmic targeting should be optimally combined in a two-stage allocation framework, in which a screening stage observes true outcomes for a subset of units before a final allocation stage assigns the resource under a fixed coverage budget. We show that the optimal strategy screens units at the margin of algorithmic allocation, while directly targeting the highest-risk units. We empirically characterize when screening and algorithmic targeting act as complements or substitutes: efficiency gains from screening grow as the aleatoric uncertainty in the population increases. Finally, we characterize the relative value of screening and direct allocation, which yields a simple rule for splitting a program budget between the two: the optimal cutoff depends only on their cost ratio. We illustrate our framework with applications in income-based social protection programs and humanitarian demining in Colombia, where the tension between screening costs and allocation efficiency is operationally consequential

signals.title: From Noise to Diversity: Random Embedding Injection in LLM Reasoning
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.11936v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent soft prompt research has tried to improve reasoning by inserting trained vectors into LLM inputs, yet whether the gain comes from the learned content or from the act of injection itself has not been carefully separated. We study Random Soft Prompts (RSPs), which drop the training step entirely and append a freshly drawn sequence of random embedding vectors to the input. Each RSP vector is sampled from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the entrywise mean and variance of the pretrained embedding table; the sequence carries no learned content, and yet reaches accuracy comparable to optimized soft prompts on math reasoning benchmarks in several settings. The mechanism unfolds in two stages: because attention has to absorb a never-seen-before random position, the distribution over the first few generated tokens flattens and reasoning trajectories branch, and as generation continues this influence dilutes naturally so the response commits to a single completion. We show that during inference RSPs lift early-stage token diversity and, combined with temperature sampling, widen Pass@N, the probability that at least one out of N attempts is correct. Beyond inference, we carry the same effect into DAPO training and demonstrate practical gains. Our contributions are: (i) RSP isolates the simplest form of soft prompt -- training-free, freshly resampled -- providing a unified lens for the structural effect of injection that variants otherwise differing in training and form all share; (ii) a theoretical and empirical validation of the underlying mechanism; and (iii) an extension from inference to training.

signals.title: Formal Conjectures: An Open and Evolving Benchmark for Verified Discovery in Mathematics
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.13171v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As automated reasoning systems advance rapidly, there is a growing need for research-level formal mathematical problems to accurately evaluate their capabilities. To address this, we present Formal Conjectures (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures), an evolving benchmark of currently 7559 mathematical problem statements formalized in Lean 4. Sourced from areas of active mathematical research, the dataset features 1642 open research conjectures without known solutions for mathematical proof discovery, 2923 solved problems for proof auto-formalization, and 2994 supporting statements. Notably, the repository provides a structured interface connecting mathematicians who formalize and clarify problems with the AI systems and humans attempting to solve them. Demonstrating its immediate utility, the benchmark has already been leveraged for new mathematical discoveries, including the resolution of open research conjectures, and for the formal confirmation of major newly announced results. We describe our approach to ensuring the correctness of these formalizations in a collaborative open-source project where contributions stem from an active community. In this framework, AI-generated proofs and disproofs serve as a valuable auditing mechanism to iteratively improve the fidelity of the benchmark. Finally, we provide a standardized evaluation setup and report baseline results on frozen evaluation subsets, demonstrating a climbable signal that measures the current frontier of automated reasoning on research-level mathematics.

signals.title: FrontierOR: Benchmarking LLMs' Capacity for Efficient Algorithm Design in Large-Scale Optimization
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.25246v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for optimization modeling and solver-code generation, yet practical operations research and optimization problems often require a harder capability: designing scalable algorithms that exploit problem structure and outperform direct formulation-and-solve baselines. Existing benchmarks are limited to small or simplified examples far below real-world scale and complexity. We introduce FrontierOR, the first literature-grounded benchmark targeting LLM-generated algorithm efficiency on realistic large-scale optimization problems. FrontierOR includes 180 diverse tasks, each derived from a paper published in a top-tier operations research venue, with standardized instances and a hidden, expert-verified evaluation suite. We evaluate recent LLMs' one-shot algorithm generation and improvements achieved through several self-evolving frameworks. The results show that current models still struggle to move from executable formulations to efficient optimization algorithms. Even the strongest LLM succeeds on only 39% of Full-set task instances, where success is defined as returning a feasible solution with an objective gap of at most 1% relative to Gurobi within its runtime. On the Hard subset, test-time evolution raises this proportion from 51% for the strongest one-shot model to 78%. FrontierOR provides a continuously maintained testbed for evaluating LLM-designed optimization algorithms under a shared protocol and controlled computational settings. Code and data are publicly released at https://github.com/Minw913/FrontierOR.

signals.title: AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.28655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific research proceeds through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and revision. AI agents can automate parts of this process, but existing approaches typically follow a single research trajectory or coordinate through a central planner with fixed objectives. As a result, they struggle to sustain parallel exploration, adapt as experimental evidence changes, or preserve knowledge of failed directions over long-running experiments. We introduce AutoScientists, a decentralized team of AI agents for long-running computational scientific experimentation. Agents interpret a shared experimental state, self-organize into teams around promising hypotheses, critique proposals before using experimental compute, and share successes and failures to reduce redundant exploration. Under matched experimental budgets, AutoScientists improves over prior AI agents across biomedical machine learning, language-model training optimization, and protein fitness prediction. On BioML-Bench, spanning biomedical imaging, protein engineering, single-cell omics, and drug discovery, AutoScientists achieves a mean leaderboard percentile of 74.4% across 24 tasks, improving over the strongest AI agent by +8.33%. On GPT training optimization, AutoScientists reaches a target validation bits-per-byte 1.9x faster than Autoresearch and continues discovering improvements from a starting champion where the single-agent approach finds none (7 vs. 0 accepted improvements). On ProteinGym fitness prediction, AutoScientists discovers a method for ACE2-Spike binding that improves over the current state-of-the-art model by +12.5% in Spearman correlation. Applied without modification across all 217 ProteinGym assays, the same

signals.title: From XXLTraffic to EvoXXLTraffic: Scaling Traffic Forecasting to Sensor-Evolving Networks
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.29768v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Traffic forecasting benchmarks commonly fix the sensor set, although deployed sensing networks change their coverage over time. We present EvoXXLTraffic, a sensor-evolving extension of the XXLTraffic dataset family, with yearly sensor catalogs, persistent station IDs, flow matrices, and geographic graph snapshots across nine California PeMS districts, spanning up to 27 years. The benchmark separates all-sensor forecasting from supervised adaptation to sensors absent from the preceding year. We evaluate 13 baseline adaptations on PEMS04 with five seeds and PEMS05 with three seeds, and seven of them on the other seven districts with three seeds. Each yearly task uses 31 stored days, explicit observation masks, and chronological evaluation. Under the frozen configurations, PECPM has the lowest full-horizon mean MAE on both all-sensor and new-node populations on PEMS04, while Online-AN leads both populations on PEMS05. Among the seven methods run on every district, Online-AN has the lowest all-sensor mean MAE in eight of the nine districts, and Online-NN has the lowest new-node mean MAE in six. A matched control on PEMS05 and PEMS06 finds that training on the evolving catalog changes mean MAE on the sensors present in every 2018-2025 catalog by less than 1% in either direction. Method ordering depends on district, evaluation population, horizon, and metric, and seed variation does not establish statistical significance. The benchmark documents implementation adaptations and uses retrospective geographic graphs, limiting claims about original-paper rankings and prospective deployment. Inherited fixed-sensor gap and hourly/daily tasks provide complementary temporal settings. Code and results: https://github.com/cruiseresearc

signals.title: POIROT: Agents as their own auditors for failure attribution in large language model multi-agent systems
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.02282v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are kept out of safety-critical domains by emergent failures that are hard to detect and to attribute. Current evaluation relies on a centralised evaluator, human or LLM judge, that must master the domain and hold the whole interaction history in one context. We propose that the agents executing a task can themselves attribute its failures. We introduce POIROT (Phased Oversight via Introspection, Review and Opinion Tallying), a modular protocol in which each agent casts a private vote within a hazard space derived from the system architecture, and the votes are aggregated into a single attribution. Before the vote, phases are added that progressively increase the interaction between agents, from independent self-assessment to sharing the self-assessments and peer interrogation. We build the protocol phase by phase, measure the contribution of each phase through an ablation, and compare every configuration with a single-LLM evaluator. We evaluate one proprietary and two open-weight LLMs on the Who&When benchmark and on BLAME (Benchmark for Localising Agent Malfunctions Effectively), a new benchmark for fault attribution in clinical rehabilitation and algorithmic trading systems. Agent-based attribution outperforms the single-LLM evaluator, but the benefit comes from independent self-assessment, not from interaction: sharing the assessments makes agents converge on the same, often wrong, culprit, and interrogation does not recover the loss. Without sharing and interrogation, the protocol outperforms the evaluator in all nine model-benchmark configurations (up to +50 percentage points). POIROT and BLAME are released as open source.

signals.title: LEAP: Supercharging LLMs for Formal Mathematics with Agentic Frameworks
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.03303v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong informal mathematical reasoning but struggle to generate mechanically verifiable proofs in formal languages like Lean. We present LEAP, an agentic framework that enables general-purpose foundation models to achieve state-of-the-art performance on automated formal theorem proving. LEAP leverages foundation model capabilities, such as informal reasoning, instruction following, and iterative self-refinement. By decomposing complex problems into smaller units, the system bridges formal proof construction with informal blueprints through continuous interaction with the Lean compiler. To provide a rigorous evaluation beyond increasingly saturated benchmarks, we introduce Lean-IMO-Bench, a benchmark of IMO-style problems formalized in Lean, with short statements yet highly non-routine and multi-step proofs across a wide range of difficulty levels. Empirically, on the latest 2025 Putnam Competition, an annual mathematics competition for undergraduate students in North America, LEAP solves all 12 problems, matching recent breakthroughs by frontier formal mathematical models. On Lean-IMO-Bench, LEAP boosts the one-shot formal solve rate of general-purpose LLMs from below 10% to 70%, notably surpassing the 48% benchmark set by a specialized, gold-medal-caliber IMO system. Furthermore, we demonstrate LEAP's research-level utility by autonomously formalizing complex proofs for open combinatorial challenges, including a verified proof for a key subproblem in Knuth's Hamiltonian decomposition of even-order Cayley graphs.

signals.title: Tree-Based Formalization of Multi-Agent Complementarity in Human-AI Interactions
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.04779v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predictive tasks constitute subprocedures within human--AI interactions (HAIs) involving professionals and AI systems. Complementarity occurs when an HAI outperforms a benchmark defined by its constituent agents. Existing formalizations, however, focus on a single human and a single AI, leaving multi-agent interactions insufficiently characterized. We introduce a tree-based mathematical framework for multi-agent complementarity. Ordered agent-role configurations decorate the leaves of rooted planar binary trees and local aggregation rules generate protocol outputs evaluated against either a best-average or a pointwise-min benchmark. We establish four results. First, under linear pooling, every protocol tree provides a bijective coordinate system for the interior of the simplex of global leaf weights. Arbitrary trees with the same ordered leaves admit output- and complementarity-preserving reparameterizations, realized locally through path-independent Tamari rotations. However, HAI constraints can violate admissibility preservation between equivalent protocols. Second, for regression under squared loss, we characterize complementarity through residual correction and derive optimal linear-pooling weights. We also characterize protocol-indifference loci under identical local parameters. Third, selector-based protocols cannot achieve complementarity relative to the pointwise-min benchmark, independently of task and loss. Fourth, in binary classification, HAIs cannot achieve complementarity under endpoint-monotone losses and the pointwise-min benchmark, with an analogous obstruction for multiclass cross-entropy. Numerical illustrations examine the main claims. We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing multi-agent p

signals.title: TRL-Bench: Standardizing Cross-Paradigm Representation-Level Evaluation of Tabular Encoders
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.09323v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tabular encoders are usually evaluated inside task-specific end-to-end pipelines, so models from different training paradigms are difficult to compare directly even when they operate on similar tabular signals. We introduce TRL-Bench, a multi-granular tabular representation learning (TRL) benchmark that standardizes cross-paradigm representation-level evaluation: each encoder exports row-, column-, or table embeddings through its supported wrapper, and shared lightweight heads probe them across three suites: TRL-CTbench (column/table), TRL-Rbench (row), and TRL-DLTE (compositional Data-Lake Table Enrichment spanning all three granularities). To support this standardized setting, we release curated benchmark assets and task reformulations, including 50 OpenML tables with 123 verified targets, 16 row-pair linkage rewrites, and a 47,772-table DLTE lake derived from 1,379 parent tables. Across 20 models and 16 tasks, TRL-Bench shows that once downstream conditions are standardized, encoder quality is capability-specific rather than captured by a single leaderboard. In TRL-CTbench, generic text encoders often lead on tasks with strong surface-text signal, while tabular specialists win where their pretraining objective aligns with the task. In TRL-Rbench, within-table prediction and cross-table linkage favor different training regimes, with atomic linkage performance correlating strongly with the row-matching stage of DLTE pipelines. In TRL-DLTE, the strongest pipelines combine capability-matched specialists rather than reuse a single encoder, and top end-to-end quality depends on non-additive compositional fit rather than per-stage marginal rank alone. TRL-Bench provides a common protocol for measuring reusable signal in ex

signals.title: Synthesizing Human Trajectory Anomalies: An LLM-Driven Framework with Map-Constrained Routing and Sensor Noise Simulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.10314v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although the study of human trajectory anomalies is vital for spatial data mining, empirical research remains constrained by the lack of ground-truth datasets. Despite the availability of several real-world and simulated human trajectory datasets, most only include normal mobility patterns and lack annotated anomalies. This limitation primarily arises because anomalous events are rare in the real world and difficult to collect. Furthermore, collecting large-scale mobility data is hindered by strict privacy regulations and acquisition costs. To overcome these limitations and establish an explainable human trajectory anomalies dataset with annotated ground truth, we introduce an end-to-end generative framework designed to synthesize context-aware trajectory anomalies at scale. Unlike existing models, our framework applies real-world physical constraints on baseline simulated trajectories. We employ Large Language Model (LLM) agents to systematically inject semantically meaningful behavioral anomalies such as irregular out-of-distribution check-ins and skipped routine visits. To ensure the spatial validity, the system leverages a map-constrained routing module to recalculate the physical transitions between these LLM agent-modified staypoints. Moreover, to narrow the simulation-to-reality gap, we augment the resulting trajectories with a context-aware spatial noise model, parameterized by environmental and location-specific variables, to emulate heterogeneous GPS sensor degradation. Through this pipeline, our framework produces a CTI & EBI formatted mobility dataset with annotated anomalies, providing a benchmark for downstream spatial data mining tasks.

signals.title: PAL-Bench: Evidence-Grounded Profile Reconstruction from Longitudinal Personal Albums
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.16175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Longitudinal personal albums are weak-schema multimodal databases: noisy perceptual records whose key facts require joins across faces, text, timestamps, locations, and repeated events. Existing visual, video, document, and lifelog benchmarks test sub-problems, but not album-scale profile reconstruction with social identity binding and evidence citation. Benchmarking this task is difficult because the ground truth needed for evaluation--owner profiles, social graphs, face-name maps, and evidence provenance--is private state that real albums cannot safely release. We introduce PAL-Bench, a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded reconstruction under a public-record contract. Its Evidence Compiler builds latent private worlds, programs target-level evidence paths, renders album pixels, re-measures them through perception pipelines, and exports audited public/private views. Agents receive only perception-derived public records; targets, identifier maps, and evidence paths remain hidden. PAL-Bench contains 50 synthetic users, 36,659 public photo records, and 2,799 targets over owner facts, identities, and relations. A privacy-preserving audit with 10 participants confirms that PAL-Bench evidence structures match real private albums, though equivalent releases remain privacy-prohibitive. Across seven systems and two compute-matched diagnostics, a seven-metric protocol reveals a gap between plausible profile summarization and faithful social reconstruction: systems recover some owner facts but struggle with recurring identities and evidence citation. PAL-TRACE, a reference framework that freezes identity bindings before owner-fact mining, performs best but leaves hard identity resolution far from solved. PAL-Bench provide

signals.title: A Contradiction Judge Counted Reported Teammate Errors as Hallucinations: An Assertion-Aware Re-Score of One Multi-Agent LLM Harness
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.21666v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM judges that score hallucination flag any statement that contradicts a reference fact. Agents in multi-agent LLM systems quote and dispute each other's claims, so such a judge can count a correct report of a teammate's error as a hallucination. An earlier version of this study, a preprint (arXiv:2606.21666v1), reported that broadcasting raised a hallucination rate from 0.492 to 0.658 (+34%) and called it contamination; this version withdraws that claim, and the preprint's runs cannot be re-scored. An unpublished revision of that harness reported 0.289 to 0.554 (+0.265, 95% CI [0.225, 0.305]), and its saved outputs are re-scored here. Under an analysis plan fixed before any judge call, three judges from three vendors labeled each of six facts in 1,832 outputs as asserted wrong, attributed to another source, asserted correct or absent. On values that outputs assert as their own, the broadcast effect was -0.0208 (95% CI [-0.0458, +0.0041]) on 10 Full-Broadcast trials: not distinguishable from zero, and equivalent to zero only within a post hoc margin of +/-0.0663 and under the plan's prompt. On these LLM-judge labels, reports of a teammate's wrong value accounted for nearly all of the Haiku travel effect. Scored for mentions, the judges reproduced the effect (+0.1996). With Llama agents, 2 of 40 teammate outputs asserted the wrong destination. One of twelve Claude judge-prompt combinations gave an asserted increase (Sonnet 4.6, one paraphrase: +0.0246, 95% CI [+0.0055, +0.0436]). In 40 new trials per arm, judged by Claude models like the agents, the asserted difference was -0.0505 when both judges agreed and +0.0161 (95% CI [+0.0024, +0.0299]) when either did. Main limit: the labels have no human validation; human labe

signals.title: Agent MechSuits: Mechanistic Subspace Safety Steering for Multi-Turn CLI Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.22673v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Command-Line Interface (CLI) agents based on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable autonomous capabilities, but they also introduce significant safety and misuse risks during multi-turn interactions with external environments. Existing safety mechanisms mainly rely on external guardrails, which have a limited ability to perform fine-grained behavioral control during execution. Meanwhile, recent mechanistic interpretability methods for LLM safety are mostly confined to single-turn or jailbreak-style QA settings, limiting their ability to capture the evolving risk dynamics of multi-turn agent execution. In this paper, we investigate the safety of multi-turn CLI agents from an internal perspective. We propose Agent MechSuits (Mechanistic Subspace Intervention and Steering), a white-box defense framework that performs runtime safety detection and representation-level mitigation for CLI agents. Unlike conventional agent guardrails, Agent MechSuits detects harmful execution states from step-level hidden representations and mitigates unsafe behavior by intervening in a 10-dimensional subspace within a single layer. To support this research, we introduce the Mechanistic Agent Safety (MAS) benchmark, comprising comprehensively annotated multi-turn execution trajectories across 194 tasks using LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Extensive experiments show that Agent MechSuits achieves strong safety detection performance, provides preliminary evidence for lookahead risk anticipation, and substantially reduces harmful actions of the CLI agent, establishing a foundation for applying mechanistic interpretability to dynamic LLM agent safety.

signals.title: World-Model Collapse as a Phase Transition
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.31399v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Water looks unchanged as it warms, then at a critical point it boils. We ask whether long-horizon language agents show an analogous transition in their ability to maintain an accurate representation of the evolving world state. In some parameter settings, a small change in a task parameter, or adding a single step to the task, leaves behavior nearly unchanged; near a critical boundary, the same small change causes a sudden collapse. We study this effect in a deterministic task family where the true world state is known at every step. A large grid search over state size, state dependency, horizon, number of available actions, observation mode, and frequency of state changes reveals a phase diagram: a low-stress region where the agent consistently succeeds, a narrow region where success drops sharply, and a high-stress region where the agent consistently fails. Step-by-step traces show the mechanism: the agent loses track of the true world before its actions become invalid, so the agent is not merely choosing a bad action; it is acting from a corrupted world. Stronger models reach the critical boundary later but do not eliminate the sharp transition. These results make world-model collapse a measurable bottleneck for long-horizon agents. Code will be made publicly available soon.

signals.title: When Can Learned Uncertainty Be Trusted? An Audit of Distributional Reinforcement Learning
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.11607v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many learned predictive models represent their uncertainty as a probability distribution, and planners and policies use this distribution to judge risk. However, the fact that a model outputs a distribution does not tell us whether that distribution captures the uncertainty in the environment which is relevant for a decision. In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_{\theta}(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. Based on these r

signals.title: Isotropy Cliffs: The Geometric Signature of Decision-Making in Large Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.00828v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the geometry of decision-making in Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA) through the lens of isotropy. Analyzing five open-weight models across diverse datasets, we identify decision-critical transition layers characterized by a shift in isotropy, coinciding with a major representational change and the emergence of task-relevant clusters. We demonstrate that this synchronized geometric behavior is strongly correlated with downstream accuracy ($r\approx0.84$), displaying its relevance for successful decision-making. Furthermore, we show that this transition is robust to prompt variations, suggesting that it reflects a general mechanism of model behavior.

signals.title: Chronocooked: A Benchmark for Interval Timing in Reinforcement Learning Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.16666v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interval timing is considered an important aspect of human cognition. As artificial agents increasingly function alongside humans, their interval timing abilities need to be studied. However, research in this area remains limited and scattered. This paper presents Chronocooked, a reinforcement learning (RL) benchmark environment that enables a systematic study of interval timing abilities in RL agents. The suite comprises cooking scenarios involving interval timing tasks inspired by psychology literature. Each task is accompanied by evaluation metrics to study different aspects of interval timing in RL agents, namely, task performance, human-like timing and scalability. We report baselines using a non-recurrent model (CNN), a recurrent model (LSTM), and a biologically inspired recurrent model (CTRNN). The CNN model showed limited ability to perform the basic timing tasks. In contrast, both recurrent models with sufficient memory successfully performed the timing tasks, exhibited temporal control in the Fixed Interval (FI) task, and qualitatively reproduced human-like psychometric curves in the Temporal Bisection task. However, no quantitative evidence of human-like timing behavior was found. A systematic study of interval timing in artificial agents may offer complementary perspectives for improving task performance in fields like human-robot interactions (HRI), while also contributing to broader research on time perception.

signals.title: UMER: Unifying Embedding and Ranking via Pair-Aware Discriminative Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Retrieval
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.18504v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern Web information access increasingly involves heterogeneous multimodal content, including images, videos and visually rich documents. Users may seek not only globally similar content but also candidates that satisfy fine-grained attributes, relations or answer evidence under complex instructions. Supporting such access requires both efficient corpus-scale retrieval and fine-grained relevance reasoning. Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based embedding methods derive representations from MLLM hidden states, and recent work further uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to improve embedding capability by injecting intermediate semantic evidence into the representation. However, existing CoT methods typically use item-wise reasoning over queries and candidates in isolation, providing no explicit evidence to distinguish a positive from a semantically confusable hard negative. Moreover, contrastive embeddings capture global similarity but struggle with meta-tasks requiring answer verification, category judgment or fine-grained reasoning. In this paper, we propose UMER, a Unified Multimodal Embedding and Ranking framework for universal multimodal retrieval. UMER replaces item-wise reflection with PairAware Discriminative Reasoning, which compares query-candidate pairs to identify instruction-relevant matching and discrepancy evidence. UMER jointly learns contrastive embeddings for efficient global matching and discriminative ranking for explicit pairwise relevance judgment within a single MLLM. A complementary mutual distillation strategy further transfers reliable pairwise preferences between the embedding and ranking functions. On MMEB-V2, UMER-R scores 65.5/70.6 with Qwen2-VL-2B/7B, outperforming the strongest i

signals.title: Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.23670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based agents execute multi-step tasks, but their behavioral structure remains opaque: long unstructured traces resist the safety auditing and runtime monitoring that deployment requires. Existing approaches operate per-trace or success-only, so they miss the cross-run topology that links next-step and failure prediction. To recover that shared structure, we collapse an entire trace corpus into a single, compact finite-state machine (FSM) that serves as a structural substrate for the otherwise unpredictable behavior of LLM agents. Across twelve public datasets, the FSMs are compact (7-43 states), replay held-out data at >=0.997 fitness with near-identical topology across splits, and build in milliseconds. This substrate addresses both prediction goals. For next-step prediction, FSM-state context outperforms Agent Workflow Memory on every ground-truth-matched dataset. For failure prediction, per-state behavioral features reach held-out AUROC up to 0.94, and an online monitor ranks failing runs above passing ones from a partial trace, triggering early stopping well before completion. Behavioral topology thus appears shaped more by the deployment harness than by the LLM, providing a model-agnostic structural primitive for safety auditing and runtime monitoring.

signals.title: AgentRoom: Concurrent Multi-Agent Coding in a CRDT-Backed Shared Workspace
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.23740v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concurrent multi-agent coding offers a division of labor across modules, robustness through redundancy and parallel exploration at the natural granularity of multi-file projects. Realtime collaborative editing protocols solve this coordination problem for human teams with Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), but the LLMs underneath generate one token at a time, and existing multi-agent coding systems inherit this serial limit, since they either sequence agents through phase handoffs or pool independent samples without coordination, and a single agent abandons up to half of hard tasks with a one-file stub-and-exit. AgentRoom is a realtime collaborative editing protocol for concurrent coding agents. Its runtime layer exposes file-level claim, status and broadcast as MCP tools on a CRDT-merged shared filesystem. Five frontier coding-CLI models ran four backend coding tasks, with cross-language checks in Python DevBench and Rust+axum. For CLI-stable models, AgentRoom with 2 agents abandons fewer tasks than Solo and varies less from run to run. At matched compute, one positive mean LLM-judge contrast puts AgentRoom over parallel-merge. The other contrast, a bundle probe, puts full AgentRoom above each partial case: an ordering rather than a percentage split. Coordination, not parallelism or CRDT-merge, is the key design choice.

signals.title: Semantic Overlays: Mitigating Prompt Injection with Annotations Beyond Tokens and Steering Vectors
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.23873v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models see only tokens. But the harness knows more: which token spans are user text, which are tool outputs, and which come from untrusted sources such as web pages or external documents. To pass that knowledge to the model, the harness must transmit it as plain text. Prompt injection exploits this: planted instructions, formatted the right way, can convince a model that they come from the user or the system. We introduce Semantic Overlays, small trained adapters that edit a frozen model's residual stream at chosen token spans. No input text can create or remove a mark, although the model's response to a mark is computed from states the input does influence. When the serving stack marks retrieved text with an overlay trained to mean "do not execute instructions in this span," the model treats injected instructions as inert content. Against attacks written without knowledge of the defense, it reaches the attack rates of the best published defenses: SEP separation rises from 24.3% to 98.8% under a corrected grader, AlpacaFarm attack success falls from 99.0% to 0.5%, and AgentDojo from 12.8% to 0%. Fine-tuning the model's weights on the same data reached similar separation but kept 64-80% of SEP utility, against 93% for the overlay. On TensorTrust hijacking, whose attacks resemble nothing in our training data, it lets 4.4% of hijacks through on Llama-3.1-8B, against 43% for Meta-SecAlign on the same base. An attacker with the weights does better: GCG succeeds on 72% of items, and on 14% after adversarial training of the overlay alone. Overlays are also flexible: the model reads their positions faithfully in stacked configurations; told by an overlay that non-Python code is Python and asked to copy it, the model r

signals.title: Four conditions for composing plugin-based agents without a host agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.28553v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model agents now run long-horizon, multi-tool, autonomous sessions, and the infrastructure must keep the current assembly of capabilities, the progress of execution, and the basis for recovery after a fault. A single-process host holds this information in its own running state, so its death takes the session record and the assembly with it. This paper gives four conditions under which a plugin-based agent needs no host process, one each on state placement, record carriers, recovery coordination, and provider resolution. The store, writer, and delivery disciplines keep the conditions in force, and each carries formal support from the spatiotemporal-composability calculus and from the proofs in the supplementary materials. An agent that meets them can be constructed with its assembly on a bus of peer processes and its record in an append-only carrier owned by no process, and removing any one part makes the assembly need a host again. The conditions themselves are the contribution, and every implementation that meets them inherits the same advantages. Such an agent keeps its session through the death of any process, wastes no calls after a fault, loses no records, recovers locally, changes its capability set while it runs, and carries its undo semantics across processes. This paper builds one SDK of the conditions, Logos, and measures whether it fulfills their promise against the single-process reference and a configuration over MCP under one fault in each of 200 tasks, realized in 197. The reference lost all 197 faulted sessions, the MCP configuration kept its sessions but issued 1,212 wasted calls, and the SDK kept every session, wasted no call, lost no record, and fulfilled the promise of the conditions

signals.title: Anchoring Clinical Events in Time: UID-Preserving Multimodal Reconstruction and Source-Grounded Adjudication
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.13062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpreting a patient's hospital course depends on when symptoms developed, tests were performed, and treatments began. Discharge summaries often leave this chronology unclear, while structured electronic health record (EHR) tables timestamp only some of these events. We reconstruct clinical timelines by retrieving structured evidence for narrative events and jointly revising their estimated times. Each extracted occurrence carries a persistent unique identifier (UID) linked to its source span, keeping repeated mentions distinct throughout reconstruction. We also introduce GAVEL, a large language model (LLM) judge that checks disagreements between two timelines against the note and structured record and cites evidence for its verdicts. We evaluated six open-weight models on 40 clinician-annotated discharge summaries. Our pipeline recovered more reference events than LLM-Timeline and TKW2 when each comparison used the same backbone. For GLM-5.2, adding structured evidence improved timestamp agreement with essentially unchanged event recovery; ablations showed that links to timestamped source rows contributed to this improvement. Results varied across the other models, with some timing gains accompanied by fewer recovered events. Both GAVEL judges, GLM-5.2 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL, favored multimodal over text-only GLM-5.2 timelines, while neither clearly distinguished the DeepSeek V3.2 variants. Manual review upheld most sampled GAVEL findings. The source links allow reconstructed times to be checked, and GAVEL identifies disagreements for human review.

signals.title: GraphSkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.20455v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: External skills provide domain knowledge and procedures without updating model parameters, but flat text makes their applicability, dependencies, and composition difficult to express. Existing skill graphs organize rules into nodes and relations mainly for retrieval and composition. They give less attention to what should change after a failure, which examples should be retested, and which edits should be reverted. We introduce GraphSkillAA, short for Graph-Skill Abductive Attribution, which connects rule use, error localization, and update validation through the same skill graph. Nodes record applicability, procedures, and exclusion conditions, while edges describe prerequisite and enhancement relations. The student records the nodes and edges used during execution. The teacher contrasts related successful and failed trajectories to identify the fields or relations that need repair, keeping changes as small as possible. Execution lapses or insufficient evidence leave the graph unchanged. A Local Gate retests affected examples, while a Big Gate checks the merged graph on the complete update pool. Rejected edits are rolled back, and model parameters remain frozen throughout. With GPT-5.6-sol, GraphSkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and achieves the highest mean performance in every main setting. These results show that graph structure supports skill selection and composition while also providing explicit targets for repair, retesting, and rollback.

signals.title: Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.20658v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

signals.title: Persona Following Is Not Selective Control: The Neutrality Gap in LLM User Simulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.35036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Persona prompting is widely used in LLM user simulation, yet it relies on an untested assumption: specifying a target user attribute should shift target behavior while leaving other fixed attributes unchanged. Across eight black-box and five open-weight models, however, changing a target attribute alone also shifts unspecified non-target choices, such as risk preference shifting color choice. We test whether explicitly specifying non-target attributes restores selective control across 477 held-out synthetic worlds and 200 independent items under unspecified, directional, and neutral states. Assigning a clear non-target direction nearly eliminates cross-attribute shifts. Explicitly declaring no preference, however, still leaves 37.7%-76.3% of held-out worlds and 51%-81% of independent non-target items shifting with the target attribute while preserving target efficacy. We call this disparity the neutrality gap. Because directional tests can be passed simply by following a stated preference, the neutral state reveals selective-control failures they miss: following a stated persona does not imply keeping unrelated choices invariant. In simulated investment decisions, incidental brochure color labels shift estimated target risk treatment effects by 25.5 percentage points, even when models accurately report having no color preference. Counterfactual attention interventions show that unwanted influence enters primarily at query time, when option evaluation reads the target persona directly. Blocking query-time attention cuts non-target drift by 72.1%-87.8%, whereas directional declarations suppress drift primarily by overwriting option values rather than rerouting attention. signals.title: Representational Simplicity and Circuit Size Dissociate in a Threshold-Dependent Way: A Controlled Test via Adversarial Training
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.35890v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse-autoencoder decomposability and concentrated feature attribution are increasingly treated as evidence that a model's computation is easier to reverse-engineer. Whether this representational and attributional cleanliness actually predicts a smaller or more tractable causal circuit remains an open question. We test this directly using adversarial training as a controlled instrument: it reliably reshapes internal representations, but this alone does not constitute a test of circuit size. We investigate this question through reverse-engineering complexity: the causal structure required to recover a model's behavior at a fixed level of faithfulness. To our knowledge, this is the first controlled empirical test of whether representational or attributional simplicity translates into causal simplicity at the circuit level. Starting from the same pretrained GPT-2 Small checkpoint, we apply matched standard and adversarial continual training, requiring both conditions to retain competence on indirect object identification and pass independent robustness verification before comparing mechanisms. We then compare the models along three complementary axes: sparse-autoencoder decomposability, SAE feature engagement in task attribution, and the size of faithful circuits recovered from the raw computational graph. The robust model is more SAE-decomposable and engages fewer SAE features in task attribution. Circuit size is regime-dependent: on competence-matched IOI, standard leads or ties below 85% faithfulness, but robust needs substantially fewer edges at high faithfulness (90%, 95%). signals.title: Multi-Task Self-Evolving Harnesses with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.38372v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks never used during evolution. We frame the evolution process as deep-learning training with two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harnesses evolved by GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol gain about 5 points on the in-distribution benchmarks, matching or exceeding Claude Code and Codex, and the GPT-5.6 Sol harness is on par with Codex on five out-of-distribution benchmarks. Continued evolution on Claw-Eval in the second stage then lifts GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3-Flash above Codex and Claude Code. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms that emerged during evolution, including output truncation, history compaction, completion check

signals.title: Do More Modalities Always Help? A Geometric Perspective on Missing-Modality Robustness
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.04792v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Missing modality remains a longstanding challenge in multimodal learning. Existing methods typically address this issue through modality recovery or adaptive strategies. However, they overlook models' internal cross-modal dependencies formed during multimodal training, which later impair robustness. We systematically characterize a counterintuitive deployment-time failure mode: models trained on full modalities can underperform unimodal models when one modality is missing at inference time. This pattern appears across diverse architectures, such as fusion models, CLIP-style two-tower models, and vision-language models. We show that such degradation is closely associated with learned cross-modal dependencies in the principal parameter subspaces. Multimodal training induces structured rotations of these subspaces, particularly in cross-modal interaction layers. These rotations are associated with reduced task-aligned margins and larger task-aware representation harm under missing-modality inputs. We propose Geodesic Unlearning (GU), a lightweight parameter-editing method that leverages Grassmannian subspace geometry for structured subspace correction to improve missing-modality robustness. It rotates the principal input subspace toward a unimodal reference along a geodesic path. We prove that this correction minimizes the distance to the reference within a fixed subspace-distance budget. Experiments across architectures and datasets show that GU improves performance under missing-modality inference while preserving full-modality accuracy, outperforming strong missing-modality robustness baselines. These findings support a geometric view of deployment-time missing-modality degradation and suggest localized subspace editin

signals.title: Which Buildings Are Artificial Intelligence-Ready? A Measurement-Based Assessment Framework for AI Question Answering and Actuation
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.09119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are becoming the interface to buildings, answering questions and controlling operations, but a building's readiness for them has not been systematically assessed. This study proposes a framework to quantify it. First, a building's knowledge graph sets two ceilings. The answerable-readiness ceiling is the share of operational questions its data could answer, and the actuation-readiness ceiling is the share of control actions it exposes. Second, a reference AI agent's accuracy on a fixed set of these questions shows how much of the ceilings is realized. On a simulated office, the agent realizes 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, so missing data, not the AI, limit readiness, except in naming a fault's cause. Across 37 public real-building graphs, the median answerable ceiling is 0.16, and in 15 of 45, unlinked sensors lower it. The framework turns "is this building AI-ready?" into an auditable, ranked retrofit question.

signals.title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.10498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

signals.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.15221v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

signals.title: Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards: Distilling Expert Traces into Programs
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.19148v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Small language models struggle with tool-use tasks that require following multi-step procedures. Whether these failures reflect limited capability or missing procedural knowledge remains unclear. We introduce Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards (PLVR), which distils expert traces into reusable programs without updating model weights. Frontier models turn recurring operations in the traces into typed primitives and rules, and search assembles them using reference actions and training-task checks. A small frozen model executes the primitives, with deterministic verifiers checking their outputs. The resulting program guides a student's reasoning or checks its proposed actions. We evaluate the same program across students on $\tau^2$-Bench Retail and Telecom and LiveMCPBench, using synthetic training tasks and unseen benchmark test tasks. On Telecom, PLVR raises an 8B model's success rate from 43.0% to 91.2%, while larger students reach up to 94.4%, compared with 57.9% for the best baseline. On Retail and LiveMCPBench, PLVR is competitive with the best baselines, although tool search remains more dependent on the student model. These results support program learning as a way to transfer expert procedures across frozen models, trading additional inference computation for more reliable tool use.

signals.title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.19423v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discov

signals.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.25096v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows.
